title: Problem Statement and Historical Context
content:
Erdős Problem #434 asks: Which k-element subset of {1,...,n} maximizes the count of non-representable integers (sums with repetition)? Kiss (2002) proved the answer is {n-k+1,...,n} (the 'top k' set).

This connects to the classical Frobenius/coin problem: given coin denominations with gcd 1, what amounts can't be made? Problem #434 goes further — it optimizes the *choice* of denominations to maximize unreachable amounts.
mathContext: \max_{A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}, |A|=k} |\{m \in \mathbb{N} : m \neq \sum a_i,\, a_i \in A\}| = |\text{NonRep}(\{n-k+1,\ldots,n\})|: The Frobenius problem dates to Frobenius (1882) and Sylvester (1884). Erdős and Graham posed the extremal variant in their 1980 monograph. Kiss solved it in 2002 in Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest.

title: Representability via Multisets
content:
**IsRepresentableAs n A** holds when n = a₁ + a₂ + ... + aₘ for some aᵢ ∈ A (repetition allowed). Formalized using `Multiset ℕ`: there exists S with all elements in A and S.sum = n.

Examples with A = {3, 5}: 6 = 3+3 (representable), 8 = 3+5 (representable), 7 (NOT representable).

This is the numerical semigroup generated by A: the set of all nonneg integer linear combinations.
mathContext: \text{IsRepresentableAs}(n, A) \iff \exists S : \text{Multiset}\,\mathbb{N},\; (\forall a \in S,\, a \in A) \wedge S.\text{sum} = n: Existential over Multiset ℕ with membership constraint (∀ a ∈ S, a ∈ A) and sum constraint (S.sum = n). The representable set forms a numerical semigroup (closed under addition, containing 0). Using multisets rather than lists or functions naturally captures the 'with repetition' aspect.

title: Zero is Always Representable
content:
**zero_representable**: 0 is representable by any set A, using the empty multiset ∅ with sum 0. Proved by `use ∅; simp`.

This is the identity element of the numerical semigroup: the empty sum convention.
mathContext: \forall A,\; \text{IsRepresentableAs}(0, A): Existential witness ∅ (empty multiset); simp handles both membership vacuity and Multiset.sum_zero. The empty sum being 0 is the standard convention in algebra.

title: Elements are Self-Representable
content:
**mem_representable**: Any element a ∈ A is representable by A, using the singleton multiset {a}. Proved by `use {a}; simp [ha]`.

This shows A ⊆ RepresentableSet(A), the generating set embeds into its semigroup.
mathContext: a \in A \implies \text{IsRepresentableAs}(a, A): Existential witness {a} (singleton multiset); simp with membership hypothesis. The generating set always embeds into the numerical semigroup it generates.

title: Sum Closure of Representability
content:
**add_representable**: If m and n are both representable by A, then m + n is too. Combine multisets Sm + Sn: membership follows from cases on Multiset.mem_add, and sum follows from Multiset.sum_add.

This proves the representable set forms a subsemigroup of (ℕ, +). Together with zero_representable, it's a submonoid.
mathContext: \text{IsRep}(m, A) \wedge \text{IsRep}(n, A) \implies \text{IsRep}(m+n, A): Destructs both existentials to get Sm, Sn; witnesses Sm + Sn; membership by cases on Multiset.mem_add; sum by simp. This closure under addition is what makes the Frobenius problem interesting: eventually all large enough integers become representable when gcd(A) = 1.

title: Non-Representable Set
content:
**NonRepresentable A** = {n : ℕ | ¬IsRepresentableAs n A}, the complement of the representable set within ℕ. When gcd(A) = 1, this set is finite (classical Frobenius theorem). When gcd(A) > 1, infinitely many integers are non-representable.

Problem #434 asks to maximize |NonRepresentable A| by choosing A optimally.
mathContext: \text{NonRep}(A) = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : n \notin \langle A \rangle\}: Set comprehension with negation of IsRepresentableAs. In numerical semigroup theory, |NonRep(A)| is called the genus of the semigroup ⟨A⟩. Problem #434 asks to maximize this genus over all k-element generating sets drawn from {1,...,n}.
prerequisites: gcd and the Frobenius (Chicken McNugget) theorem

title: Counting Non-Representables
content:
Two counting functions: **countNonRepresentable** (ℕ∞-valued via Set.encard, handles infinite case) and **nCardNonRepresentable** (ℕ-valued via Set.ncard, returns 0 for infinite sets).

Both are noncomputable. The ncard version is used in Kiss's theorem since the interesting case has gcd = 1 (finite non-representables).
mathContext: g(A) = |\text{NonRep}(A)| = |\{n \in \mathbb{N} : n \notin \langle A \rangle\}|: Set.encard for extended natural cardinality (handles infinite case when gcd(A) > 1); Set.ncard for natural cardinality (returns 0 when infinite). Using both cardinalities is a design choice: encard is semantically correct for all cases, while ncard is more convenient for the finite comparisons in Kiss's theorem.

title: Frobenius Number
content:
**frobeniusNumber A** = sSup(NonRepresentable A), the largest non-representable integer. Well-defined when gcd(A) = 1 (the set is finite and bounded). For coprime a, b: frobeniusNumber {a,b} = ab - a - b (Sylvester 1884).

Note: Problem #434 maximizes the COUNT, not the Frobenius number itself. Problem #433 focuses on maximizing the Frobenius number.
mathContext: F(A) = \max(\text{NonRep}(A)) = \text{sSup}(\{n : n \notin \langle A \rangle\}): sSup (supremum) of NonRepresentable A; relies on the set being bounded above when gcd(A) = 1. The Frobenius number and genus are related but distinct invariants of a numerical semigroup.

title: Complete Sets (gcd = 1)
content:
**IsComplete A** holds when A is nonempty and gcd(sSup A, sInf(A \ {sSup A})) = 1. Complete sets have finitely many non-representable integers.

The Chicken McNugget theorem is a famous example: {6, 9, 20} has Frobenius number 43.
mathContext: \text{IsComplete}(A) \iff A \neq \emptyset \wedge \gcd(\sup A, \inf(A \setminus \{\sup A\})) = 1: Nat.gcd applied to sSup and sInf of the remainder set; a simplified coprimality check. The Chicken McNugget theorem (for {6, 9, 20}) became a popular math puzzle. For 3+ elements, computing the Frobenius number is NP-hard (Ramírez-Alfonsín 2005).

title: The topK Set: {n-k+1, ..., n}
content:
**topK n k** = Set.Icc (n - k + 1) n, the k largest elements of {1,...,n}. This is the conjectured (and proved) optimal choice for maximizing non-representables.

Examples: topK 5 2 = {4, 5}, topK 10 3 = {8, 9, 10}. The greedy construction greedyConstruct equals topK by definition (rfl).
mathContext: \text{topK}(n, k) = \{n-k+1, n-k+2, \ldots, n\} = [n-k+1, n] \cap \mathbb{N}: Set.Icc (closed interval) from n-k+1 to n. Natural number subtraction requires care (n - k + 1 for k > n wraps to 1). The topK set is the unique optimal solution to the extremal Frobenius problem.

title: The Extremal Frobenius Question
content:
**ExtremalFrobeniusQuestion n k**: For all A ⊆ {1,...,n} with |A| = k, nCardNonRepresentable(A) ≤ nCardNonRepresentable(topK n k). This is the formal statement that topK is optimal.

Kiss (2002) proved this is true for all valid n, k.
mathContext: \forall A \subseteq [1,n],\; |A| = k \implies g(A) \leq g(\text{topK}(n,k)): Universal quantification over sets A with subset and cardinality constraints; comparison via ≤ on nCardNonRepresentable. This is the extremal formulation: topK achieves the maximum genus among all valid generating sets.

title: Small Examples: {2,3}, {3,5}, topK(5,2)
content:
Three concrete examples illustrate the pattern:
- **{2, 3}**: NonRepresentable = {1}, Frobenius number 1. Small numbers → few gaps.
- **{3, 5}**: NonRepresentable = {1, 2, 4, 7}, Frobenius number 7. By Sylvester: 3·5 - 3 - 5 = 7, count = (2)(4)/2 = 4.
- **topK(5, 2) = {4, 5}**: Proved by ext + simp + omega. Many more non-representables.

The topK example has far more non-representables, illustrating why larger numbers are optimal.
mathContext: g(\{2,3\}) = 1, \quad g(\{3,5\}) = 4, \quad g(\{4,5\}) = 6: example_2_3 and example_3_5_frobenius are sorry'd; topK_5_2 proved via ext, simp [topK, Set.Icc], omega. The progression from g({2,3})=1 to g({4,5})=6 illustrates how larger generators create more gaps. By Sylvester's formula, g({n-1,n}) = (n-2)(n-1)/2, growing quadratically.

title: Kiss's Theorem (2002): topK is Optimal
content:
**kiss_2002**: For 1 ≤ k ≤ n, ExtremalFrobeniusQuestion n k holds — the set {n-k+1,...,n} maximizes nCardNonRepresentable among all k-element subsets of {1,...,n}.

This is the main result, axiomatized because Kiss's proof requires detailed analysis of representation counts via generating functions and comparison inequalities for different subsets.
mathContext: \forall n \geq 1, \forall k \in [1,n],\; \text{ExtremalFrobeniusQuestion}(n, k): Stated as axiom; the proof requires generating function analysis and combinatorial comparison arguments. Kiss (2002) published the result in Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest. Eötvös Sect. Math., pp. 139-142. The proof analyzes how replacing a small element with a larger one affects the count of non-representable integers.

title: Problem #434 Answer: YES
content:
**erdos_434_answer**: Direct corollary of kiss_2002. For all valid n, k and any A ⊆ {1,...,n} with |A| = k, nCardNonRepresentable(A) ≤ nCardNonRepresentable(topK n k).

Proved by exact application of kiss_2002.
mathContext: \text{erdos\_434\_answer} := \text{kiss\_2002}(n, k, h_n, h_k, h_{kn}): Direct application: kiss_2002 n k hn hk hkn. The answer to Erdős Problem #434 is YES: the topK set is optimal.

title: Larger Numbers Create More Gaps
content:
**larger_numbers_fewer_reps**: For n ≥ 2, nCardNonRepresentable({n-1, n}) > nCardNonRepresentable({1, 2}). Since {1, 2} represents everything (all positive integers), while {n-1, n} leaves many gaps.

With {1, 2}: all positive integers are representable. With {9, 10}: 1-8 are all non-representable, plus 11-17, etc.
mathContext: g(\{n-1, n\}) = \frac{(n-2)(n-1)}{2} > 0 = g(\{1, 2\}) \quad \text{for } n \geq 2: Sorry'd; would follow from sylvester_count since {1,2} has genus 0 (every positive integer is a sum of 1s and 2s) and {n-1,n} has genus (n-2)(n-1)/2 > 0 for n ≥ 2. This is the intuitive core of why topK is optimal: larger generators space out representable integers more widely.

title: Sylvester-Frobenius Theorem and Count Formula
content:
Two classical results axiomatized:
- **sylvester_frobenius**: For coprime a, b > 0, frobeniusNumber {a,b} = ab - a - b.
- **sylvester_count**: The count of non-representables is (a-1)(b-1)/2.

For {3, 5}: Frobenius number = 15 - 3 - 5 = 7, count = (2)(4)/2 = 4.

**consecutive_count** (sorry): For consecutive integers {n-1, n}, the count is (n-2)(n-1)/2, growing quadratically.
mathContext: F(\{a,b\}) = ab - a - b, \quad g(\{a,b\}) = \frac{(a-1)(b-1)}{2} \quad (\gcd(a,b)=1): Both stated as axioms. Sylvester proved both results in 1884. The Frobenius formula ab-a-b is elementary but requires careful case analysis of which integers ax + by (x,y ≥ 0) can reach. The count formula (a-1)(b-1)/2 follows by observing that exactly half of the integers in [0, ab-a-b] are non-representable, by a symmetry argument.

title: Greedy Construction Equals topK
content:
**greedyConstruct n k** = Set.Icc (n - k + 1) n, identical to topK by definition. **greedy_eq_topK**: proved by rfl.

The greedy algorithm (always pick the largest available number) naturally produces the topK set, and Kiss's theorem shows this greedy approach is optimal.
mathContext: \text{greedyConstruct}(n, k) = \text{topK}(n, k) \quad (\text{by } \texttt{rfl}): Definition is identical to topK; equality proved by rfl (definitional equality). The greedy algorithm is optimal — a rare case where the simple greedy approach gives the provably best answer. This contrasts with most combinatorial optimization problems where greedy is suboptimal.

title: Finiteness of Non-Representables
content:
**nonrep_finite**: When A has two coprime elements, NonRepresentable A is finite. **topK_finite**: For k ≥ 2 and n ≥ k, NonRepresentable(topK n k) is finite.

Both are sorry'd. The classical result: if gcd(A) = 1, then all sufficiently large integers are representable (the Frobenius number bounds the non-representable set).
mathContext: \gcd(A) = 1 \implies |\text{NonRep}(A)| < \infty: Sorry'd; would need the Schur/Frobenius theorem that gcd=1 implies finitely many non-representables. The proof idea: if gcd(a,b) = 1, then by Bézout's identity, some linear combination ax + by = 1, and from this all sufficiently large integers are representable.

title: Connection to Problem #433
content:
**problem433Set n k** = Set.Icc n (n + k - 1), the consecutive integers {n, n+1, ..., n+k-1}. Problem #433 maximizes the Frobenius number for this specific form; #434 maximizes the non-representable count over all k-subsets.

**frobenius_consecutive** (axiom): The Frobenius number for consecutive integers is (n-1)(n+k-1)/k - 1.
mathContext: F(\{n, n+1, \ldots, n+k-1\}) = \frac{(n-1)(n+k-1)}{k} - 1: Set.Icc for consecutive integer range; frobenius_consecutive axiomatizes the Frobenius number formula. Problems #433 and #434 are companion extremal problems from the same Erdős-Graham 1980 monograph: #433 optimizes the Frobenius number, #434 optimizes the genus.

title: Complete Answer: topK is Optimal
content:
**erdos_434_complete**: For all n ≥ 1, k ≥ 1, k ≤ n, and any A ⊆ {1,...,n} with |A| = k: nCardNonRepresentable(A) ≤ nCardNonRepresentable(topK n k).

Proved by exact application of kiss_2002. This is the definitive answer to Erdős Problem #434.
mathContext: \forall n, k, A,\; 1 \leq k \leq n,\; A \subseteq [1,n],\; |A|=k \implies g(A) \leq g(\text{topK}(n,k)): Direct application of kiss_2002 axiom with all parameters. This is the definitive formalization of the solution to Erdős Problem #434.

title: topK Achieves Maximum (IsGreatest)
content:
**topK_is_maximum**: Formulates the result using Mathlib's `IsGreatest`: topK achieves the maximum of {nCardNonRepresentable A | A valid}. Sorry'd — requires showing topK is itself valid (⊆ {1,...,n} with |topK| = k) and applying kiss_2002.

This is the strongest formulation: not just 'all others are ≤' but 'topK is in the set AND is the greatest'.
mathContext: \text{IsGreatest}(\{g(A) : A \subseteq [1,n], |A|=k\},\; g(\text{topK}(n,k))): IsGreatest over the image set requires two components: membership (topK is a valid k-subset of {1,...,n}, which needs topK_card) and maximality (from kiss_2002). Sorry'd because topK_card itself is sorry'd.
